title: The Mauryan Empire

cards.b: The Mauryas (c. 321 to 185 BCE) united most of the subcontinent. We have rich sources: Kautilya, Megasthenes, Ashoka’s edicts. Ashoka’s Dhamma is a regular Mains theme.

• Arthashastra (Kautilya or Chanakya; dating disputed, between c. 300 BCE and 300 CE, with the core from Mauryan times).
  • Indica (Megasthenes, Greek ambassador at Chandragupta’s court; survives in fragments).
  • Mudrarakshasa (Vishakhadatta, Gupta period).
  • Buddhist texts (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa), Jain texts, Ashokan inscriptions, Rudradaman’s Junagadh inscription (Sudarshana lake).

Chandragupta Maurya (c. 321 to 297 BCE), with Chanakya, overthrew the Nandas, defeated Seleucus Nicator (c. 305 BCE; treaty gave Kabul, Kandahar, Herat and Baluchistan for 500 elephants; Megasthenes sent). Later, tradition says he became a Jain monk (Shravanabelagola). Bindusara (c. 297 to 273 BCE): “Amitraghata” (slayer of foes); extended to the Deccan; ties with Syria (Antiochus I) and Egypt.

Ashoka (c. 268 to 232 BCE). Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE; Rock Edict XIII: 100,000 killed, 150,000 deported): he turned to Buddhism and Dhamma. Edicts in Brahmi (and Kharosthi, Greek, Aramaic in the west) on rocks and pillars; discovered by James Prinsep (1837 deciphered Brahmi). Rock Edicts, Minor Rock Edicts, Pillar Edicts (Delhi-Topra, Sarnath), Lauriya Nandangarh. He is called “Devanampiya Piyadasi”.

Not a new religion but a moral code: tolerance, non-violence to animals, respect to elders, kindness to slaves, truth, generosity. Dhamma-mahamattas (appointed in the 13th year) took the message; tours (dhamma-yatras), welfare (wells, trees, hospitals, rest houses), peace with neighbours, envoys to Sri Lanka (Mahinda and Sanghamitra), Syria, Egypt, Macedonia. Ashokan lion capital at Sarnath is India’s emblem; the wheel is on the flag. Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra.

Highly centralised. Saptanga (seven limbs of the state). King; mantri-parishad; Amatyas; 18 tirthas (officials) in the Arthashastra. Provinces: Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali, Suvarnagiri, Pataliputra (Kumaras as governors). Local: Gopa, Sthanika; Pradeshika, Rajuka, Yukta. Megasthenes: six committees of five members each in Pataliputra. A vast spy network (gudhapurushas). A standing army (600,000 infantry per Pliny). Revenue: bhaga (one-sixth), bali, sita (crown lands), taxes on trade; state control of mines and the economy.

Agriculture, state farms (sita), irrigation (Sudarshana lake), trade by Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha, punch-marked coins, guilds. Material: NBPW. Slaves (dasa), foreigners (Yavanas). Pataliputra was among the largest cities. Decline: weak successors, an expensive army and bureaucracy, tax pressure, Ashoka’s policies, provincial revolts, the rise of regions; Pushyamitra Shunga killed Brihadratha, the last Maurya (c. 185 BCE).

Romila Thapar (Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas, 1961) shows Dhamma as a policy of social cohesion in a diverse empire. D. D. Kosambi and R. S. Sharma see Mauryan state as exploitative. Ashoka’s non-violence is also debated: he did not disband the army or end the death penalty. The Arthashastra’s realism (Kautilya) vs Ashoka’s idealism is a classic comparison.

The Ashoka Chakra is on the flag and the Lion Capital is the State Emblem; “Satyameva Jayate” is added beneath. Ideas of welfare state, ethical governance and tolerance (Article 25) are often linked to Dhamma. The Arthashastra shapes India’s strategic thought; Pataliputra’s remains lie under Patna. Ashokan edicts are Brahmi examples in UNESCO’s tentative list.
